extracted.intended_audience: employers, human resources and payroll professionals, labor attorneys, compliance officers, and other stakeholders affected by or implementing the FLSA EAP exemptions
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory criteria and standards in the Department of Labor's final rule (29 CFR part 541) for determining when executive, administrative, professional, outside sales, and computer employees are exempt from the FLSA minimum wage and overtime requirements. Includes salary-basis, salary-level, duties tests, HCE test, updating mechanisms, dates, and analytic metrics used to assess impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary basis test
rubrics_metrics.description: The employee must be paid a predetermined and fixed salary that is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of work performed (the salary basis test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the three longstanding prongs for the EAP exemption (salary basis, salary level, duties). The rule reiterates that the salary must be fixed and not reduced for quantity/quality variations; employers must ensure pay arrangements meet this requirement to claim the exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard salary level test
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of salary paid must meet a minimum specified amount (the salary level test). The Department is setting the standard salary level at the 35th percentile of weekly earnings of full‑time salaried workers in the lowest‑wage Census Region ($1,128 per week or $58,656 annually for a full‑year worker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This salary level works together with the standard duties test to identify bona fide EAP employees. The Department selected the 35th percentile methodology to 'fully restore the salary level's screening function' while accounting for the one‑test system. Applicability date for the new standard salary level is January 1, 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties test (standard duties test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The employee's job duties must primarily involve executive, administrative, or professional duties as defined by the regulations (the duties test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties—not job titles or pay alone—determine exemption status. The standard duties test is paired with the standard salary level; it replaces the prior long/short two‑test structure and requires an analysis of actual job functions against regulatory definitions of executive, administrative, and professional duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly Compensated Employee (HCE) test
rubrics_metrics.description: A streamlined alternative combining a very high total annual compensation requirement with a minimal duties test. The Department is increasing the HCE total annual compensation threshold to the annualized weekly earnings of the 85th percentile of full‑time salaried workers nationally ($151,164).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCE test is intended to be reserved for employees 'at the very top of [the] economic ladder' and uses minimal duties scrutiny because high compensation is a strong indicator of exempt status. The new HCE threshold applicability date is January 1, 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer burden of proof for claiming exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer bears the burden of establishing the applicability of the exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must be prepared to demonstrate compliance with the salary basis, salary level, and duties requirements; mere job titles or paying a salary do not suffice to establish exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job titles and job descriptions are not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Job titles and job descriptions do not determine EAP exemption status, nor does merely paying an employee a salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual duties and pay arrangements control; employers should analyze real day‑to‑day functions against regulatory duties definitions rather than rely on labels or compensation form alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial update (July 1, 2024) to salary and HCE thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule establishes an initial updating of the standard salary level and the HCE total annual compensation threshold on July 1, 2024, using the methodologies in place at that time (the 2019 rule methodologies), resulting in a $844 per week standard salary level and a $132,964 HCE total annual compensation threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These initial updated amounts take effect July 1, 2024; the new standard salary level and HCE threshold adopted in this final rule become applicable January 1, 2025, per the rule's stated applicability schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triennial updating mechanism for salary and compensation thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Future updates to the standard salary level and HCE total annual compensation threshold will begin 3 years after the initial update (July 1, 2027) and every 3 years thereafter, using the methodologies in place at the time of the updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule adopts a regulatory provision to allow timely, predictable, and efficient updating of thresholds with current earnings data. The mechanism includes features (and an exception) to pause future updates under certain conditions; the updates use whatever methodology the Department has in place at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale and methodology selection for salary level
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department selected a methodology that sets the standard salary level at the 35th percentile of weekly earnings of full‑time salaried workers in the lowest‑wage Census Region to restore the salary level's screening function and account for the switch from a two‑test to a one‑test system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule balances prior approaches (2004/2019 vs. 2016) to avoid over‑inclusion of lower‑paid workers who perform significant nonexempt work while retaining benefits of a simplified one‑test system. The document discusses alternative methodologies, concerns (e.g., 'ratcheting'), and the policy reasons for the percentile and regional choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of salary as a screening tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The salary level serves a screening function to help identify who is employed in a bona fide EAP capacity, limiting the inclusion of lower‑paid workers who perform significant nonexempt work in the exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that a well‑calibrated and regularly updated salary level, together with duties tests, reduces litigation and helps ensure nonexempt employees receive overtime protections; long intervals between updates erode the effectiveness of the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with state law (nonpreemption and higher state standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some state laws have stricter standards (e.g., higher salary levels or more stringent duties tests) than the FLSA; the FLSA does not preempt such stricter state standards. If a state establishes a higher standard, the higher standard applies in that state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must comply with both federal and any applicable state requirements and apply the more protective standard where state law is stricter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical long and short tests (nonexempt‑work cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, the part 541 regulations had a long test paired with a lower salary level and a cap on nonexempt work (introduced as a 20 percent cap in 1940) and a short test paired with a higher salary level and less rigorous duties test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule explains this history to justify the chosen methodology and the role of the salary level in combination with duties tests; the historical 20% cap on nonexempt work informed prior two‑test structures and the Department's analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and effective dates
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective date for this final rule is July 1, 2024. Sections 541.600(a)(2) and 541.601(a)(2) are applicable beginning January 1, 2025. The new standard salary level and HCE threshold have applicability dates described in the preamble (standard salary level applicability date noted as January 1, 2025).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders must track specific section applicability dates; some provisions (e.g., certain salary thresholds) take effect on different dates as described in the rule text and preamble. The Department did not finalize certain proposals (e.g., applying the standard salary level to U.S. territories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of highly compensated employees who do not meet standard duties test
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who currently are exempt under the HCE test but do not meet the standard duties test may lose exemption if their total annual compensation falls below the new HCE threshold; absent employer pay increases to meet the new HCE level, their exemption status will turn on the standard duties test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department estimated the number of workers affected and explains that employers may need to increase pay or otherwise reclassify affected workers; the preamble quantifies impacts (e.g., estimated number affected) to inform compliance planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic impact assessment metrics and required analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule's analytical framework evaluates number of affected EAP workers, characteristics of affected workers, costs (regulatory familiarization, adjustment, managerial), transfers (income shifts from employers to employees), sensitivity analyses, and distributions by industry/region/demographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department provides tables, figures, and modeling (e.g., Tables 2–27, Figures 1–9) to quantify impacts, projected costs and transfers, and alternatives. Employers and stakeholders can use these metrics to estimate likely effects and compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and paperwork considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule discusses projected reporting, recordkeeping, and other compliance requirements of the rule and references recordkeeping regulations (e.g., 29 CFR 516.3) which provide that employers need not maintain certain records for EAP workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FRFA and Paperwork Reduction Act sections evaluate additional compliance burdens; agencies and employers should consult the referenced recordkeeping rules to determine which records remain required and which are excepted for EAP workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special salary levels and U.S. territories
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department is not finalizing in this rule its proposal to apply the standard salary level to U.S. territories subject to the Federal minimum wage and is not finalizing updates to special salary levels for American Samoa and the motion picture industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains these exclusions and the rationale for not applying the new standard salary to territories or changing industry‑specific special levels in this final rule; stakeholders in those jurisdictions/industries should monitor future rulemaking.
